summary.text: For Pell pairs defined by $(P_0,Q_0)=(0,1)$ and $(P_{r+1},Q_{r+1})=(P_r+Q_r,2P_r+Q_r)$, the identities $Q_r^2-2P_r^2=(-1)^r$ and their parity consequences show that the sign pattern is preserved by odd-indexed Pell shifts and by twice an even-indexed shift, but reversed by an even-indexed shift; the resulting cancellation proves that each initial block of length $P_{2j+1}$ has sum $1$. Defining $N_0=0$ and $N_{j+1}=N_j+P_{2j+1}$, a Pell growth bound $N_j\le P_{2j+1}$ lets the preserved-block identity apply inductively, giving $a(N_j)=j$.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 c(k)=(-1)^{\lfloor k(\sqrt2-1)\rfloor}\qquad(k\ge 1)
\]
and
\[
 A(n)=\sum_{k=1}^n c(k),\qquad A(0)=0.
\]
Thus it is enough to construct, for every nonnegative integer \(j\), an index \(N_j\) such that \(A(N_j)=j\).

We begin with a Pell sequence. Define integer pairs \((P_m,Q_m)\) by
\[
 (P_0,Q_0)=(0,1),
\]
\[
 P_{m+1}=P_m+Q_m,\qquad Q_{m+1}=2P_m+Q_m.
\]
The first few pairs are
\[
(0,1),(1,1),(2,3),(5,7),(12,17),\ldots.
\]
We shall need the following elementary properties.

First,
\[
 Q_m^2-2P_m^2=(-1)^m. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed it holds for \(m=0\), and the recurrence gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
Q_{m+1}^2-2P_{m+1}^2
&=(Q_m+2P_m)^2-2(Q_m+P_m)^2\\
&=-(Q_m^2-2P_m^2).
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (1) by induction. The same recurrence also shows that \(P_m\ge0\), \(Q_m>0\), and \(P_m>0\) for \(m>0\).

Second, reduction modulo \(2\) gives
\[
 P_m\equiv m\pmod 2,\qquad Q_m\equiv1\pmod2. \tag{2}
\]
This follows by induction from
\(P_{m+1}=P_m+Q_m\) and \(Q_{m+1}=Q_m+2P_m\).

We next express the exponent in \(c(k)\) in a form suited to Pell approximations. For a positive integer \(k\), let
\[
 x=\lfloor k\sqrt2\rfloor.
\]
Then \(x>0\), and
\[
 x^2\le 2k^2<(x+1)^2. \tag{3}
\]
The right inequality is immediate from \(x<k\sqrt2<x+1\). The left one follows from \(x\le k\sqrt2\). Equality \(x^2=2k^2\) cannot occur: it would give \(\sqrt2=x/k\), contrary to the irrationality of \(\sqrt2\). (The usual proof of irrationality is that if \(x^2=2k^2\) with a fraction \(x/k\) in lowest terms, then \(x\) is even, and substitution then forces \(k\) to be even as well.) Hence the integer
\[
 D=2k^2-x^2
\]
satisfies \(D\ge1\). Likewise, because the quantities are integral,
\[
 E=(x+1)^2-2k^2\ge1. \tag{4}
\]
Also \(k\le x\): otherwise \(x+1\le k\), which would give
\((x+1)^2\le k^2<2k^2\), contradicting (3).

Subtracting \(k\) from
\(x\le k\sqrt2<x+1\) gives
\[
 x-k\le k(\sqrt2-1)<x-k+1.
\]
Consequently
\[
 \lfloor k(\sqrt2-1)\rfloor=x-k. \tag{5}
\]
In particular this exponent is nonnegative.

We now prove the three translation facts that drive the argument.

**Translation lemma.** Suppose \(k,P,Q,x\) are positive integers and (3) holds.

1. If
\[
Q^2=2P^2-1\quad\hbox{and}\quad k\le P,
\]
then
\[
\lfloor (k+P)\sqrt2\rfloor=x+Q. \tag{6}
\]

2. If
\[
Q^2=2P^2+1\quad\hbox{and}\quad k\le P,
\]
then again
\[
\lfloor (k+P)\sqrt2\rfloor=x+Q. \tag{7}
\]

3. If
\[
Q^2=2P^2+1\quad\hbox{and}\quad 2k^2\le P^2-1,
\]
then
\[
\lfloor (k+2P)\sqrt2\rfloor=x+2Q. \tag{8}
\]

We prove these assertions by checking the two consecutive-square inequalities that characterize the floor.

For part 2, first observe that
\[
(xQ)^2=x^2(2P^2+1)\le (2kP)^2.
\]
Indeed, since \(D\ge1\), we have \(x^2\le2k^2-1\), and hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^2(2P^2+1)
&\le (2k^2-1)2P^2+x^2\\
&=4k^2P^2-2P^2+x^2\\
&\le4k^2P^2,
\end{aligned}
\]
because \(x^2\le2k^2\le2P^2\). All quantities are nonnegative, so
\[
xQ\le2kP. \tag{9}
\]
Similarly,
\[
(2kP)^2\le((x+1)Q)^2. \tag{10}
\]
For example, using \(2k^2\le x^2+2x\), the difference between the right and left sides is at least zero after substituting \(Q^2=2P^2+1\); explicitly,
\[
\begin{aligned}
((x+1)Q)^2
&=(x+1)^2(2P^2+1)\\
&\ge (2k^2+1)(2P^2+1)>4k^2P^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Now expand the desired lower difference:
\[
\begin{aligned}
2(k+P)^2-(x+Q)^2
&=(2k^2-x^2)+2(2kP-xQ)+(2P^2-Q^2)\\
&=D+2(2kP-xQ)-1\ge0
\end{aligned}
\]
by \(D\ge1\) and (9). For the upper difference,
\[
\begin{aligned}
(x+Q+1)^2-2(k+P)^2
&=((x+1)^2-2k^2)
 +2((x+1)Q-2kP)+(Q^2-2P^2)\\
&=E+2((x+1)Q-2kP)+1>0
\end{aligned}
\]
by (10). Thus
\[
(x+Q)^2\le2(k+P)^2<(x+Q+1)^2,
\]
which proves (7).

For part 1, where \(Q^2=2P^2-1\), one obtains in exactly the same way
\[
xQ\le2kP. \tag{11}
\]
Indeed,
\[
x^2Q^2=x^2(2P^2-1)\le 2P^2x^2\le4k^2P^2.
\]
This is enough for the lower bound, since
\[
\begin{aligned}
2(k+P)^2-(x+Q)^2
&=D+2(2kP-xQ)+(2P^2-Q^2)\\
&=D+2(2kP-xQ)+1>0.
\end{aligned}
\]
For the upper bound there is one small case split. If \(k\le P-1\), then
\[
2kP<(x+1)Q. \tag{12}
\]
To see this, use \((x+1)^2\ge2k^2+1\) to obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
((x+1)Q)^2-(2kP)^2
&\ge(2k^2+1)Q^2-4k^2P^2\\
&=Q^2-2k^2\\
&=2P^2-1-2k^2\\
&\ge2P^2-1-2(P-1)^2=4P-3>0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because both sides of (12) are nonnegative, the strict square inequality implies (12). Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
(x+Q+1)^2-2(k+P)^2
&=E+2((x+1)Q-2kP)-1>0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here both \(E\) and the positive integer \((x+1)Q-2kP\) are at least \(1\).

It remains to handle \(k=P\). In that case
\[
x^2\le2P^2=Q^2+1
\]
and
\[
Q^2+1=2P^2<(x+1)^2.
\]
For positive integers \(x,Q\), the first inequality implies \(x\le Q\), while the second implies \(Q<x+1\), hence \(Q\le x\). Thus \(x=Q\). Directly,
\[
2(k+P)^2=8P^2=4(Q^2+1)<(2Q+1)^2=(x+Q+1)^2,
\]
since \(Q>0\) (and in this Pell setting the only relevant values have enough positivity; equivalently the displayed inequality reduces to \(4<4Q+1\)). This completes part 1.

For part 3, assume \(2k^2\le P^2-1\). We first have the strict inequality
\[
xQ<2kP. \tag{13}
\]
Indeed,
\[
\begin{aligned}
(2kP)^2-(xQ)^2
&=4k^2P^2-x^2(2P^2+1)\\
&=2P^2(2k^2-x^2)-x^2\\
&\ge2P^2-x^2\\
&\ge2P^2-2k^2\\
&\ge P^2+1>0.
\end{aligned}
\]
We also have
\[
2kP<(x+1)Q. \tag{14}
\]
For
\[
\begin{aligned}
((x+1)Q)^2-(2kP)^2
&=(x+1)^2(2P^2+1)-4k^2P^2\\
&=2P^2((x+1)^2-2k^2)+(x+1)^2>0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Now
\[
\begin{aligned}
2(k+2P)^2-(x+2Q)^2
&=D+4(2kP-xQ)+(8P^2-4Q^2)\\
&=D+4(2kP-xQ)-4\ge1,
\end{aligned}
\]
because both \(D\) and the positive integer \(2kP-xQ\) are at least \(1\). Also
\[
\begin{aligned}
(x+2Q+1)^2-2(k+2P)^2
&=E+4((x+1)Q-2kP)+(4Q^2-8P^2)\\
&=E+4((x+1)Q-2kP)+4>0.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (8), and hence the translation lemma.

We apply the lemma to the Pell pairs. Formula (1) says
\[
Q_{2r+1}^2=2P_{2r+1}^2-1,
\qquad
Q_{2r}^2=2P_{2r}^2+1. \tag{15}
\]
Combining (5), the translation lemma, and the parities (2) gives the following sign identities.

For every \(r\ge0\) and \(1\le k\le P_{2r+1}\), part 1 gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\lfloor(k+P_{2r+1})(\sqrt2-1)\rfloor
&=(x+Q_{2r+1})-(k+P_{2r+1})\\
&=(x-k)+(Q_{2r+1}-P_{2r+1}).
\end{aligned}
\]
Both \(P_{2r+1}\) and \(Q_{2r+1}\) are odd, so their difference is even. Therefore
\[
c(k+P_{2r+1})=c(k). \tag{16}
\]

For \(r>0\) and \(1\le k\le P_{2r}\), part 2 similarly gives an exponent differing from the old exponent by
\(Q_{2r}-P_{2r}\). Here \(P_{2r}\) is even and \(Q_{2r}\) is odd, so that difference is odd. Consequently
\[
c(k+P_{2r})=-c(k). \tag{17}
\]

There is one further repeating-block identity. For \(r>0\) and
\(1\le k\le P_{2r-1}\), we claim that the hypothesis of part 3 holds with \(P=P_{2r}\):
\[
2k^2\le P_{2r}^2-1. \tag{18}
\]
Indeed, by (15), positivity implies \(P_{2r-1}\le Q_{2r-1}\): if instead \(Q_{2r-1}<P_{2r-1}\), then \(Q_{2r-1}+1\le P_{2r-1}\), which is incompatible with
\(Q_{2r-1}^2=2P_{2r-1}^2-1\). Hence
\[
P_{2r}=P_{2r-1}+Q_{2r-1}\ge2P_{2r-1}.
\]
Thus
\[
P_{2r}^2\ge4P_{2r-1}^2\ge2k^2+1,
\]
where the final extra \(1\) is available because \(P_{2r-1}>0\) and all quantities are integral. This proves (18).

Part 3 now says that shifting \(k\) by \(2P_{2r}\) shifts \(x\) by \(2Q_{2r}\). The exponent in (5) therefore changes by
\[
2Q_{2r}-2P_{2r}=2(Q_{2r}-P_{2r}),
\]
which is even. Hence
\[
c(k+2P_{2r})=c(k)
\quad(1\le k\le P_{2r-1}). \tag{19}
\]

We now turn these sign identities into statements about partial sums. Whenever a block of length \(K\) beginning after position \(R\) repeats the initial block, we have
\[
A(R+K)=A(R)+A(K). \tag{20}
\]
If it is the negative of the initial block, then
\[
A(R+K)=A(R)-A(K). \tag{21}
\]
These formulas simply split the sum at \(R\) and reindex the second block by \(k\mapsto R+k\).

Taking \(R=K=P_{2r}\) in (17), for \(r>0\), gives
\[
A(2P_{2r})=A(P_{2r})-A(P_{2r})=0. \tag{22}
\]

Next we show that every odd-indexed Pell length has partial sum \(1\):
\[
A(P_{2r+1})=1\qquad(r\ge0). \tag{23}
\]
For \(r=0\), \(P_1=1\), and
\[
0<\sqrt2-1<1,
\]
so \(c(1)=(-1)^0=1\), proving \(A(P_1)=1\).

For \(r>0\), the Pell recurrence implies
\[
P_{2r+1}=2P_{2r}+P_{2r-1}. \tag{24}
\]
Indeed,
\[
P_{2r+1}=P_{2r}+Q_{2r},
\]
while
\[
P_{2r}=P_{2r-1}+Q_{2r-1},
\qquad
Q_{2r}=Q_{2r-1}+2P_{2r-1};
\]
substitution gives (24). Split the sum at \(2P_{2r}\). Its first part is zero by (22), and its remaining block, of length \(P_{2r-1}\), is identical to the initial block by (19). Therefore
\[
A(P_{2r+1})=A(2P_{2r})+A(P_{2r-1})=A(P_{2r-1}).
\]
Repeatedly reducing the odd index reaches \(P_1\), proving (23).

Finally define a sequence of indices by
\[
N_0=0,
\qquad
N_{j+1}=N_j+P_{2j+1}. \tag{25}
\]
We claim simultaneously that
\[
N_j\le P_{2j+1} \tag{26}
\]
and
\[
A(N_j)=j. \tag{27}
\]

For (26), the case \(j=0\) is immediate. If \(N_j\le P_{2j+1}\), then
\[
N_{j+1}\le2P_{2j+1}.
\]
On the other hand the recurrence and positivity give
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_{m+2}
&=P_{m+1}+Q_{m+1}\\
&=(P_m+Q_m)+(2P_m+Q_m)\\
&=3P_m+2Q_m\ge2P_m.
\end{aligned}
\]
With \(m=2j+1\), this yields
\(2P_{2j+1}\le P_{2j+3}\), proving the induction step for (26).

For (27), the case \(j=0\) is \(A(0)=0\). Suppose \(A(N_j)=j\). By (26), identity (16) applies for every \(1\le k\le N_j\), so the block of length \(N_j\) immediately following position \(P_{2j+1}\) repeats the first \(N_j\) signs. Since addition is commutative, (25) and (20) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
A(N_{j+1})
&=A(P_{2j+1}+N_j)\\
&=A(P_{2j+1})+A(N_j)\\
&=1+j,
\end{aligned}
\]
where (23) was used in the last line. This proves (27) for all \(j\).

Thus the sequence of partial sums actually assumes every nonnegative integer value: \(A(N_j)=j\). Given any integer \(M\), choose a nonnegative integer \(j>M\); for instance, take \(j=M+1\) if \(M\ge0\), and \(j=0\) if \(M<0\). Then
\[
A(N_j)=j>M.
\]
Therefore the sequence of partial sums of \((-1)^{\lfloor k(\sqrt2-1)\rfloor}\) is unbounded above.
